idiom_name: Read-only @property plus frozen dataclass and name-mangled holders
implementation_notes: Python has no access control - the tutorial states that private instance variables do not exist - so the pattern becomes a descriptor plus convention: a `@property` without a setter raises `AttributeError: property ... has no setter` on assignment, `@dataclass(frozen=True)` installs `__setattr__`/`__delattr__` that raise `FrozenInstanceError` for every field, and a double-underscore holder such as `self.__data` is name-mangled to `_Class__data` so a subclass assigning `self.__data` creates its own attribute instead of overwriting the base state. None of that stops `object.__setattr__`, `vars()` or `dataclasses.replace`, so treat it as protection against accidental writes. The classic Data class shows up as a small frozen dataclass or NamedTuple held in a private attribute when several fields must be validated and copied together.
pitfalls: `frozen=True` is not deep: a frozen dataclass holding a list still allows `append`, so use tuples or `MappingProxyType`, or re-freeze mutable fields in `__post_init__`.
`object.__setattr__`, `vars()` edits and `dataclasses.replace` bypass every Python-level guard; name mangling is documented as being designed 'mostly to avoid accidents', not to enforce privacy.

A class-level property cannot be shadowed by an instance attribute, which surprises code that tries to assign the name in `__init__`, and `__slots__` (the other immutability aid) is incompatible with class-level defaults.
